area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can judge a soft or rough landing surface, work out a realistic landing distance for it, and fly a stabilized soft-field approach within commercial tolerances (approach speed within 5 knots), holding the airplane just off the surface with power, touching down at the slowest possible speed with the nose wheel off, and rolling on to firm ground without getting stuck.
why: Grass, dirt, snow and mud strips are where many commercial jobs take you, and they forgive nothing: a dropped nose wheel can dig in, and a stop in the wrong spot can bog the airplane down [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

warmup: Think first: on a hard runway you finish the landing with the brakes. On a muddy grass strip the FAA says to stay off the brakes and maybe even add power after touchdown. Why would anyone add power after landing?

key_terms.def: A surface such as snow, sand, mud or tall grass that can grab the wheels or let them sink [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
An uneven surface that puts large stresses on the landing gear [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Moving the airplane's weight from the wings to the wheels slowly, using back-elevator pressure and power [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
The slope of a runway in percent. A 3 percent gradient changes height 3 ft for every 100 ft of length [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
A field condition NOTAM. Braking action FICON NOTAMs are only used for non-paved runways, taxiways and aprons [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]].
The difference between the steady wind and the gusts. Add no more than half of it to the approach speed [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Less induced drag close to the surface, felt most below one wingspan, so extra speed turns into a long float [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].
The spot your constant-angle glide path points at. It does not move in the windshield [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
The runway length you may use under a LAHSO clearance, published in the Chart Supplement [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].
An airplane on the ground turning into the wind, because it has more side area behind the main gear [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

chunks.title: The soft-field landing at commercial standards

body.p: Snow, sand, mud and tall grass need their own landing technique. The goal is to touch down as smoothly as possible at the slowest possible speed, and to let the wings carry the weight as long as practical. That protects the gear on a rough surface and keeps the wheels from sinking into a soft one [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

The approach looks like a normal approach. The big difference is that you keep some power on through the level-off and the touchdown. The airplane flies 1 to 2 feet above the surface in ground effect while the speed slowly bleeds off. When the wheels first touch, the wings still hold much of the weight, so the sudden nose-over force at touchdown is small [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

head: Short-field landing
Soft-field landing
rows: POH speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus no more than half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]
Slightly steeper when obstacles are present [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]
No reason for a steep angle unless obstacles are present [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Little or no float; touchdown at minimum controllable airspeed [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]
Held 1 to 2 ft up with some power while the speed bleeds off [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
No brakes; you may even need more power to keep moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]

body.p: Flaps help you touch down at minimum speed and are recommended whenever practical. In a low-wing airplane, mud, stones or slush thrown up by the wheels can damage them. If you used flaps, leave them down on the rollout: full control of the airplane matters more than cleaning up [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

What is different at the commercial level? The maneuver is the same, but the examiner holds you to a tighter speed window. The private standard allows +10/-5 knots on approach (ACS PA.IV.D.S7). The commercial standard is plus or minus 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7). The fast side no longer has room to hide.

callout.text: The POH/AFM speeds, flap settings and procedures come first. Where the AFH and the manufacturer differ, the manufacturer's recommendations take precedence [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

check.q: What two things does the soft-field technique protect?
check.a: The landing gear, from the stress of a rough surface, and the wheels, from sinking into a soft surface. The wings carry the weight as long as practical to do both [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

chunks.title: Read the surface before you commit

body.p: Performance charts usually assume a paved, level, smooth and dry runway. Real runways are concrete, asphalt, gravel, dirt or grass, and the Chart Supplement lists the surface for each one [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

bullets: Tires can sink into soft, grassy or muddy runways, and potholes or ruts stop them from rolling smoothly [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Mud, snow and standing water reduce tire friction, but they also act as obstructions and can shorten the landing roll [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
The surface also changes braking effectiveness. When less than ideal conditions are reported, make sure the runway is long enough [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Slope: landing uphill usually shortens the roll and landing downhill lengthens it. The Chart Supplement gives the slope [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
Water or ice can cost you all braking if the tires hydroplane [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
Check NOTAMs: a FICON NOTAM for braking action is only used for non-paved runway surfaces, taxiways and aprons [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]].

body.p: Picking the touchdown spot: choose a point that suits the wind, the surface and any obstructions (ACS CA.IV.D.S5). On a soft field, think past the touchdown. If the surface is bad you may keep the main wheels just touching while the wings carry the weight until you reach a good taxi surface [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], and stopping on mud or snow can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. So look for the firmest strip and a clear path to firm ground.

callout.text: An uneven surface or a soft spot that slows one main wheel can start a swerve that grows into a ground loop, especially in a tailwheel airplane [[24:294|AFH 14-8]].
Commercial habit: brief the surface out loud before the pattern. Surface type, slope and direction, latest NOTAM, where you will touch down, and where you will exit onto firm ground.

check.q: Why can mud or standing water shorten a landing roll even though they reduce tire friction?
check.a: They act as obstructions that hold the airplane back [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

chunks.title: Landing distance on grass: run the numbers

body.p: Anything that changes your landing speed or how fast you slow down changes the landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. You land at the same indicated airspeed in any wind, so the wind's main effect is on your groundspeed at touchdown [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

Read the notes on that sample chart. For a dry grass runway, it tells you to add 20 percent of the 'total to clear 50 ft obstacle' figure to both the ground roll and the total. It also takes 10 percent off for every 4 knots of headwind [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]]. Your own POH may use a different correction, so always use the one for your airplane.

head: Factor
Effect on landing distance
rows: Every 10 ft above 50 ft at the threshold

body.p: Energy grows with the square of speed. An airplane rolling at 75 knots has four times the energy it has at 37 knots, so it needs about four times the distance to stop [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. On a soft field you are not braking, so the surface itself has to soak up that energy [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

The factors add up. A runway that is long enough for each problem alone can be too short for all of them together [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.10]]. Operators are told to add a safety margin of at least 15 percent to a computed landing distance [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]; it is a good personal habit for you too.

callout.text: POH distances assume you touch down within a set air distance. If you float past it, you may not get the landing distance you calculated [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]].
Small airplanes often have no tailwind data. One example the FAA gives: the Cessna 150 and 152 charts say to add 10 percent for each 2 knots of tailwind, up to 10 knots [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.9.1]].

check.q: Using the sample chart at sea level on a dry grass runway, what is the total distance to clear a 50 ft obstacle?

chunks.title: Stabilized approach and energy, inside 5 knots

body.p: A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point, at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. The aiming point stays still in the windshield. If it moves up toward the horizon, the real aiming point is closer than you think and you will land short. If it moves down, away from the horizon, you will land long [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

The runway's shape is your second cue. On a steady glide path its shape does not change. If the approach gets shallow, the runway looks shorter and wider; if it gets steep, it looks longer and narrower [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

Energy management means pitch and power together. Going long: reduce power and lower the nose to hold airspeed, and add flaps if you have more [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Going short: add power and raise the nose together [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Raising the nose alone to stretch the glide makes the airspeed decay and leads to a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Low and slow on the back side of the power curve, you may need a lot of power [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

Speed: fly the short-field final approach speed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. That is the POH speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO without one, plus no more than half the gust factor in gusty air [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Then hold it within plus or minus 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7). With a gust factor added, do not let the indicated airspeed decay below the recommended landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

head: AFH stabilized approach item
Target for a typical piston airplane
rows: About a constant 3 degrees to the touchdown zone, obstructions permitting
Tracks the centerline; bank normally 15 degrees or less on final
AFH: +10/-5 KIAS. Commercial checkride: plus or minus 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7)
Generally 500 to 1,000 fpm; if over 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 ft AGL
Right for the configuration, not below the AFM minimum approach power
Done before the approach, except the landing checklist

body.p: Table source: [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

callout.text: Gates: not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC, go around. In a typical piston pattern, go around right away if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

check.q: No POH speed is published and VSO is 48 knots. The wind is calm. What is the highest planned approach speed, and what band does the commercial ACS allow around it?
check.a: 1.3 x 48 = 62.4, so about 62 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Plus or minus 5 knots gives about 57 to 67 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7).

chunks.title: Power, ground effect and the float

body.p: Close to the ground, induced drag drops. With the wing one-tenth of its span above the ground, induced drag falls by 47.6 percent [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. The effect is felt most below a height equal to the wingspan, and any extra speed at the flare turns into a long float [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].

The soft-field landing uses ground effect on purpose. Some power plus ground effect lets you hold the airplane just off the surface while it slows [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. The PHAK also notes that ground effect adds lift, so power has to come back somewhat near the ground or the airplane climbs above the glide path [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]]. The power you carry is a small, steady amount, not your approach power.

bullets: A small amount of power sends more air over the elevator, so you keep pitch authority at low speed. At idle, a windmilling propeller can block that airflow and make the flare hard [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Power adds lift without more angle of attack and slows the sink rate. Propwash over the wing gives an instant lift boost [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].
Slightly high in the landing attitude? Hold the attitude and add a little power to ease the airplane down [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].
Never close the throttle quickly near the ground. It can cause an immediate jump in sink rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Ground effect makes the elevator less effective and the nose harder to raise. Trim matters [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

callout.text: Pitch holds the nose-high attitude. Power sets how gently the weight goes onto the wheels. You use both together to control the weight transfer [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
A 6-inch free fall onto the surface is roughly a 340 fpm descent, and the load at touchdown can be three or four times the airplane's weight [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. Minimum sink rate is the whole point.

check.q: Why does a small amount of power make the soft-field flare easier at very low speed?
check.a: It blows more air over the elevator, so the elevator keeps its authority. At idle a windmilling propeller can block that airflow [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and what the examiner checks)

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH gives the real speeds, flap settings and power settings.

bullets: 1. Before the pattern: surface, slope, NOTAMs and corrected landing distance briefed; touchdown spot and exit route chosen [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]] [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]].
2. Within about 10 miles: monitor CTAF and self-announce; then downwind, base and 'On final for runway [XX]' [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]] [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
3. Downwind: gear down if retractable, and before-landing check done before base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
4. Base and turn to final: coordinated, no skid, and be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees this low [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
5. Final: verify the runway number and alignment; scan from the aiming point to the horizon, along the runway and short of it [[24:175|AFH 9-4]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
6. Landing flaps, short-field speed plus half the gust factor, trimmed. Hold it within 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7) [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
7. Crosswind: wing-low, rudder keeps the nose on the centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
8. Round out and level off 1 to 2 ft above the surface with some power still on [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
9. Touch down on the main wheels at the lowest possible airspeed, nose high, no drift [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
10. Hold back pressure to keep the nose wheel off; use back pressure and power to control the weight transfer [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
11. Once committed, lower the nose wheel gently with a slight addition of power. No brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
12. Keep moving with enough power until you reach firm ground [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Any time it is not stable or not safe: go around. Power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Manufacturer's approach speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus or minus 5 knots, with gust factor applied (ACS CA.IV.D.S7)
Recommended configuration, airspeed and trim; pitch and power adjusted to stay stabilized (ACS CA.IV.D.S6)
A suitable point for the wind, surface and obstructions. No distance tolerance is given for this Task (ACS CA.IV.D.S5)
Smooth, timely inputs; nose wheel off until the elevator loses effectiveness; proper pitch, minimum sink, no side drift, aligned with the center of the runway (ACS CA.IV.D.S9, S10)
Elevator as the manufacturer recommends; leave the soft area at a speed that keeps you from sinking; proper control positions and enough speed to keep taxiing (ACS CA.IV.D.S11, S13)
Timely, whenever the approach goes outside these standards or anything makes it unsafe (ACS CA.IV.D.S12)

check.q: In this flow, which two steps are the real difference from a normal landing?
check.a: Keeping some power on through the level-off and touchdown so the airplane floats 1 to 2 ft up [[24:194|AFH 9-23]], and holding the nose wheel off with no brakes after touchdown [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

body.p: Tricycle gear: after the main wheels touch, hold enough back-elevator pressure to keep the nose wheel off. Back pressure and power together control how fast the weight moves from the wings to the wheels [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

bullets: On a bad surface, you may keep the main wheels just touching while the wings still carry the weight, until you reach a suitable taxi surface [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Until the weight is on the wheels and the nose wheel is down, you can still add full power and take off, if obstacles and field length allow [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Once committed, lower the nose wheel gently. A slight addition of power usually helps ease it down [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Brakes are not needed and should be avoided. They load the nose gear and can make the nose wheel dig in [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
On a very soft field you may need more power just to keep moving and not get stuck [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

body.p: Taxiing on the soft surface (S13): keep the airplane in continuous motion with enough power, because stopping on mud or snow can bog it down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. It takes more power to start moving or start a turn than to keep going [[24:56|AFH 2-19]], which is one more reason not to stop.

Wind still matters on the ground. Quartering headwind: upwind aileron up. Quartering tailwind: elevator down and upwind aileron down, so the wind cannot get under the tail and wing and nose the airplane over [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. In a nosewheel airplane the elevator is normally held neutral in a headwind; in a tailwheel airplane it is held full aft [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

Tailwheel airplanes: the tailwheel touches with or just before the main wheels, then firm back-elevator pressure holds it down for the whole roll. That fights any nose-over tendency. Again, no brakes, and maybe more power [[24:294|AFH 14-8]].

callout.text: Exiting at a towered field: leave at the first available taxiway, and do not stop or reverse course on the runway without ATC approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]. At a non-towered field the FAA discourages back-taxiing because of landing traffic [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.2]].

check.q: You are taxiing a nosewheel airplane across wet grass with a quartering tailwind from the left. How do you hold the controls?
check.a: Elevator down and left (upwind) aileron down, and keep rolling with enough power [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

chunks.title: Crosswind and gusts on a soft field

body.p: There are two crosswind methods. The crab needs precise timing: you remove it with rudder just before touchdown, and too early or too late puts a side load on the gear. The wing-low (sideslip) method is recommended in most cases, and you should be able to fly both. On a long final you can crab first and change to wing-low before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

Wing-low: rudder lines the nose up with the runway; aileron gives just enough bank to stop the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. That keeps the ground track and the longitudinal axis on the centerline through touchdown and rollout [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

bullets: As you slow in the round out, the controls get weaker. Add rudder and aileron to hold the same correction, and keep the upwind wing down [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
With wing-low, the upwind main wheel touches first; the downwind main settles as the airplane slows [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Rudder-linked nose wheel steering: relax the rudder as the nose wheel touches, or it will swerve you [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
On the rollout the airplane wants to weathervane. Keep adding aileron into the wind; hold it fully into the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
Touching down while drifting creates side load. As little as 10 degrees of cornering angle makes a side load equal to half the weight on that tire [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

body.p: Gusts: use partial flaps and a power-on approach slightly faster than normal, such as normal speed plus half the gust factor (70 knots with 15-knot gusts becomes 77 knots). Close the throttle only after the main wheels touch [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. On a soft field you are already carrying power through touchdown, so plan for the extra float that the higher speed brings [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

Limits: airplanes are tested to be controllable in a 90-degree crosswind up to 0.2 VSO, and airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962 show the demonstrated crosswind on a placard [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn at the bank you need, the wind is too strong for that runway. Use a better runway, here or somewhere else [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

check.q: Your airplane's VSO is 55 knots. What crosswind was it shown to handle during certification?

chunks.title: Tailwind, wind shear and wake turbulence

body.p: Tailwind: you land at the same airspeed, so a tailwind raises your groundspeed at touchdown. The first 10 knots of tailwind add about 21 percent to the landing distance, and many small-airplane POHs give no tailwind data at all [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. With no braking on a soft field, that extra groundspeed is all rolling distance.

Wind shear is a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a small area. A headwind that turns into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst is the worst kind: often 1 to 2 miles across, lasting 5 to 15 minutes, with downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots. Virga at cloud base and a ring of blowing dust may be the only clues [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

In the figure, the headwind at X balloons the airplane, the downdraft at Y makes it sink, and the tailwind at Z robs its airspeed [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. If you reduced power and lowered the nose for the headwind, you are nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits, and you can stall or land short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. Watch for clues early and be ready to go around at the first sign; some microbursts cannot be escaped at low altitude [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. The AWH rule for an encounter: do not let pitch fall below the normal range, and accept a lower airspeed [[28:268|AWH 22-13]].
Airports with LLWAS, ITWS or WSP wind shear detection are listed in the Chart Supplement under Weather Data Sources [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7]]. Most grass strips have none, so your eyes are the detector.

Wake turbulence is strongest behind aircraft that are heavy, clean and slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]]. A crosswind of 1 to 5 knots can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone, and a tailwind can move vortices forward into it. The light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

bullets: Landing behind a larger aircraft, same runway: stay at or above its final approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].
Landing behind a larger aircraft that just departed: land well before its rotation point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].
After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go: wait at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

callout.text: Avoid the area below and behind a wake-generating aircraft, especially at low altitude, where even a short encounter could be catastrophic [[34:151|AIM 7-4-5]]. A soft-field float puts you at the lowest, slowest point of the flight.

check.q: A larger airplane has just taken off from your runway. Where should you plan to touch down?
check.a: Well before its rotation point, so you stay clear of its wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

body.p: A go-around is a normal maneuver. Hazards on the runway, overtaking another airplane, wind shear, wake turbulence and an unstable approach are all good reasons to break off [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. What makes it dangerous is waiting too long. The two usual causes of delay are landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: Step
What to do
rows: Full or maximum allowable power, smoothly and at once; carburetor heat off if applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Expect a pitch-up and left yaw. Use forward pressure and right rudder, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Once the descent stops, raise flaps in small steps; retract gear only after a positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

body.p: The soft-field go-around starts from the worst spot: slow, low and in ground effect. Ground effect performance is borrowed and you pay it back as you climb out, so climbing too soon may leave you unable to climb at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. If the airplane settles and bounces in a very low go-around, keep it straight and hold a constant, safe pitch; the added power cushions the next contact [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Even after the mains touch, you can still take off while the nose wheel is off and the wings carry the weight, if field length and obstacles allow [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

Stall and spin traps: many power-on stall accidents happen during go-arounds, from a nose-high trim setting or raising the flaps too early [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]]. High pitch, high power and low speed is the classic setup for P-factor yaw and a spin if you do not hold the rudder [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

LAHSO (land and hold short): accept only if you are sure you can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]. ALD is in the Chart Supplement, the PIC has final authority, and you are expected to decline if it would compromise safety [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Once accepted, you must follow it like any clearance, but it does not prevent a rejected landing; if you go around, keep clear of other traffic and tell the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. LAHSO needs at least a 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]]. The soft-field technique avoids the brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], so a short ALD is a poor match for it.

callout.text: Set your go-around triggers before final: not stable by the gate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], outside 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7), or not able to land in the first third of the runway or drifting sideways [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

check.q: Why should you not pull up and climb hard the instant you start a go-around from the soft-field float?
check.a: Ground effect performance is borrowed. Climbing out too soon may leave the airplane unable to climb or even hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

chunks.title: Traffic, the right runway, low-altitude traps and distractions

body.p: Collision hazards: aircraft on final or landing have the right-of-way. When two are landing, the lower one has it, but may not use that to cut in front of the other [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. The FAA discourages VFR straight-in approaches; if you fly one, announce 8 to about 10 miles out, and know that it gives you no priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].

Radio calls at a non-towered field: monitor and self-announce about 10 miles out [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]], then call each leg ending with 'On final for runway [XX]' [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. Avoid the words 'to' and 'for' where they could be mistaken for runway numbers or altitudes [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.3]].

Right runway (S3): wrong-surface landings come from an unfamiliar airport, complacency or fatigue. Study the airport diagram first, check the runway number and alignment on every final, and go around if in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Scan the runway and the area around it for traffic and obstructions (S4), from the aiming point to the horizon, along the sides and well short of the runway [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

Stall and spin: many power-off stall accidents come from crossed-control turns from base to final, and from trying to stop a high sink rate on final with pitch alone [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]]. Be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees in the turn to final and never skid it with rudder [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

CFIT and illusions: CFIT is one of the top four causes of fatal GA accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Grass strips set up classic illusions. A narrower-than-usual runway, an upsloping runway or upsloping terrain, and terrain made featureless by snow all make you feel higher than you are, so you fly too low. Haze does the same [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

Distractions: get checklists done early so your eyes are outside on final [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Many distractions start as a small problem and cause accidents when the pilot stops flying the airplane. If you are task saturated, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. In the pattern that often just means: go around.

callout.text: Aviate, navigate, communicate. In the float, flying the airplane is the only job.

check.q: You are on final to a narrow grass strip that slopes uphill, and you feel high. What is likely happening?
check.a: Both the narrow-runway and the upslope illusions make you feel higher than you are, so you risk flying too low [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Trust the aiming point and runway shape cues [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

body.p: The AFH lists these common soft-field approach and landing errors [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]:

bullets: Too much descent rate on final.
Too much airspeed on final.
Unstable approach.
Rounding out too high above the surface.
Poor power management in the round out and touchdown.
Hard touchdown.
Poor control of the weight transfer from wings to wheels.
Letting the nose wheel 'fall' instead of lowering it.

head: Problem
Fix
rows: Flaps, less power and a lower nose, or a forward slip. A sink rate over 800 to 1,000 fpm is excessive; go around if it gets there [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Add power while still high enough to get the right speed back; too slow and too low, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Hold the attitude until it starts to settle, maybe add a little power; if the nose needs to come down a lot, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Ease into the landing attitude as it settles; not down in the first third or drifting, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Power to cushion it and close the throttle after touchdown; with a crosswind, lower the wing more; excessive, go around [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]
Very slight: power to cushion and set the attitude. Severe or getting worse: go around at once [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
The nose wheel can dig in. Hold back pressure and stay off the brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]

callout.text: Pulling power to idle in the flare out of habit is the classic soft-field mistake. It can cause an immediate increase in sink rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

check.q: Name the two listed errors that are about the moments right after touchdown.
check.a: Poor control of the weight transfer from wings to wheels, and letting the nose wheel fall instead of controlling its descent [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-24. Soft/rough field approach and landing. (AFH 9-23)
f1.alt: An airplane descends on a blue glide path toward a brown dirt strip, levels off a little above the surface in a zone marked Ground effect, floats along it, and touches down nose-high in a smaller zone marked Transition area.

f2.caption: Figure 11-32. Landing distance table. (PHAK 11-27)
f2.alt: A sample landing distance table for a 1,600 lb airplane at 60 mph with flaps 40 degrees, power off, hard surface and zero wind. Ground roll and total to clear a 50 ft obstacle: sea level 445 and 1,075 ft; 2,500 ft 470 and 1,135 ft; 5,000 ft 495 and 1,195 ft; 7,500 ft 520 and 1,255 ft. Notes: subtract 10 percent per 4 knots of headwind, add 10 percent per 60 degrees F above standard, and for a dry grass runway add 20 percent of the total-to-clear figure to both distances.

f3.caption: Figure 9-7. Change in runway shape if approach becomes narrow or steep. (AFH 9-6)
f3.alt: Three cockpit views of runway 25. Too high: the runway looks long and narrow. Proper descent angle: a normal trapezoid. Too low: the runway looks short and wide, squashed toward the horizon.

f4.caption: Figure 2-15. Control positions of the nosewheel airplane. (AFH 2-20)
f4.alt: Top view of an airplane in a circle split into four colored quarters, each with a wind arrow. Wind from the front quarters: use up aileron on that wing and neutral elevator. Wind from the rear quarters: use down aileron on that wing and down elevator.

f5.caption: Figure 9-17. Crosswind approach and landing. (AFH 9-17)
f5.alt: A high-wing airplane flies down a straight blue path to a runway with the wind arrow and windsock off to the right. It holds the upwind wing low all the way to touchdown, lands on the upwind main wheel first, and rolls out on the centerline.

f6.caption: Figure 22-13. Landing in a Microburst (AWH 22-11)
f6.alt: An aircraft on a red glideslope flies under a microburst. At X a headwind balloons it above the glideslope, at Y in the center a downdraft makes it sink, and at Z a sudden tailwind costs it airspeed so it hits the ground short of the runway.

scenario.title: The sloping turf strip on a gusty afternoon
scenario.setup: You are preparing for your commercial checkride and fly with your CFI to a non-towered airport at 3,000 ft elevation with a 2,600 ft turf runway, 9/27. The Chart Supplement shows the runway slopes down toward the east, so landing on runway 9 is downhill. The wind is 300 at 10 gusting 18. A FICON NOTAM reports medium braking action on the turf, and a local pilot says the middle of the strip is soft after rain. Your POH approach speed is 61 KIAS. Your CFI wants a real soft-field landing and a full stop.

questions.q: Which runway do you pick, and why?
questions.a: Runway 27. The wind favors it, and landing uphill usually shortens the landing roll [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. Runway 9 would add a tailwind (the first 10 knots add about 21 percent) and a downhill slope (about 10 percent for each 1 percent) [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.7]] [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]].

questions.q: What approach speed do you fly, and what is your window?
questions.a: The gust factor is 8 knots; add half, 4 knots, to 61 for a 65-knot target [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. The commercial window is plus or minus 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7), and with a gust factor applied the AFH says not to let the speed decay below the 61-knot landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: How do the NOTAM and the local report change your plan?
questions.a: They tell you the surface is wet and soft, so tires can sink and braking is poor [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Plan to touch down on the firm first part, keep the nose wheel off, use no brakes, and keep moving with power to firm ground; stopping on the soft part could bog you down [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

questions.q: On final over rising terrain toward the uphill runway, you feel high and want to pull power. What should you check first?
questions.a: An upsloping runway and upsloping terrain make you feel higher than you are, so you may fly too low [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Check the aiming point and the runway shape; if the aiming point is still, you are on the glide path [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

questions.q: In the float a gust balloons you about 10 ft and the speed is falling. What do you do?
questions.a: Ballooning: add power to cushion the descent and keep the crosswind correction, lowering the wing more if needed. If it is excessive or you start to drift, go around right away [[24:204|AFH 9-33]].

questions.q: After a good touchdown the wheels start to drag in the soft middle of the strip and the nose wants to drop. What now?
questions.a: Hold back pressure to keep the nose wheel off, add power to keep moving, and stay off the brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Keep rolling until you reach firm ground [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist on time, before reaching base leg.
skills.practice: Run the checklist out loud on every downwind and finish it before turning base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

skills.do: Make the right radio calls at a non-towered field, or follow tower instructions.
skills.practice: Practice the self-announce about 10 miles out and each pattern call, ending with 'On final for runway [XX]' [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]] [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

skills.do: Make sure you are lined up with the correct or assigned runway.
skills.practice: Study the airport diagram before the flight and check the runway number and alignment on every final [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Scan the landing runway and nearby area for traffic and obstructions.
skills.practice: Scan from the aiming point to the horizon, along both sides and well short of the runway, on every final [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Pick and aim for a touchdown point that fits the wind, the surface and any obstructions.
skills.practice: On base, say your aiming point and your exit to firm ground out loud; watch the aiming point stay still in the windshield [[24:176|AFH 9-5]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

skills.do: Set the recommended configuration, airspeed and trim, and use pitch and power to stay stabilized.
skills.practice: Fly approaches to the same picture, correcting with pitch and power together rather than pitch alone [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Hold the POH approach speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus or minus 5 knots, with the gust factor applied.
skills.practice: Brief the target and the 10-knot window before final; have your CFI call out every time you drift more than 3 knots off [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and the right crosswind correction through the approach, touchdown and rollout.
skills.practice: Fly wing-low down the runway at a safe height, then on full-stop landings, adding control as you slow [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

skills.do: Make smooth, timely round-out inputs, and keep the nose wheel off until the elevator loses effectiveness.
skills.practice: Practice holding the airplane 1 to 2 ft up with a little power, then holding back pressure after touchdown [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

skills.do: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude with minimum sink rate, no side drift, aligned with the center of the runway.
skills.practice: Do low passes in ground effect down a long runway to learn the attitude and power needed, then full landings [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

skills.do: Use the elevator as the manufacturer recommends on rollout and leave the soft area at a speed that keeps you from sinking in.
skills.practice: On a real grass strip with your CFI, keep the nose light, avoid the brakes and add power as needed to keep rolling [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

skills.do: Go around on time if the approach goes outside these standards or anything makes it unsafe.
skills.practice: Have your CFI call go-arounds at random, including in the float, and fly power, attitude, configuration without climbing out of ground effect too soon [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

skills.do: Hold the proper control positions and keep enough speed to keep taxiing on the soft surface.
skills.practice: Taxi on grass in continuous motion with your CFI, using the wind control positions for the wind you have [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

quiz.q: What is the commercial ACS tolerance on soft-field approach speed?
quiz.why: The commercial standard is the published speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus or minus 5 knots with the gust factor applied (ACS CA.IV.D.S7). The private standard is +10/-5 (ACS PA.IV.D.S7). The 1.3 VSO and half-gust rules come from [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

quiz.q: In a low-wing airplane landing on a slushy strip, what flap risk does the AFH mention?
options: Flaps make the nose wheel dig in
Mud, stones or slush thrown up by the wheels can damage them
Flaps cannot be used below 1,000 ft
quiz.why: Flaps help you touch down at minimum speed, but in low-wing airplanes they may be damaged by mud, stones or slush thrown up by the wheels [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: A FICON NOTAM reports braking action on a turf runway. Where can these braking action NOTAMs be used?
options: Only when the tower is open
Only on non-paved runways, taxiways and aprons
quiz.why: FICON NOTAMs for braking action are only used for non-paved runway surfaces, taxiways and aprons [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]].

quiz.q: A runway has a 2 percent gradient. How much does its height change over 1,500 ft of length?
quiz.why: A gradient in percent is feet of height change per 100 ft of runway. 2 ft per 100 ft x 15 = 30 ft [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

quiz.q: You cross the threshold at 70 ft instead of the 50 ft the POH assumes. About how much longer will the landing be?
quiz.why: Every 10 ft above the standard 50 ft adds about 200 ft. 20 ft extra = 400 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

quiz.q: Why does extra speed on a soft-field final make the landing harder?
options: It causes a long float in ground effect, which makes a smooth touchdown harder
It makes the stall warning sound
It adds drag in ground effect
quiz.why: Higher approach speeds cause excess float in ground effect, and floating makes a smooth, controlled touchdown even more difficult [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Ground effect reduces drag, so the extra speed is slow to go away [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].

quiz.q: During the soft-field touchdown, what controls how fast the weight moves from the wings to the wheels?
quiz.why: Using back-elevator pressure and engine power, the pilot controls the rate at which the weight is transferred from the wings to the wheels [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: Taxiing a tailwheel airplane into a moderate headwind, where is the elevator normally held?
quiz.why: In tailwheel airplanes the elevator is held full aft to hold the tail down, unless the headwind is very strong. In nosewheel airplanes it is held neutral [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

quiz.q: With the wing-low method in a left crosswind, which wheel touches first?
quiz.why: With wing-low, the upwind wing is down and the initial touchdown is on the upwind main wheel [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

quiz.q: A larger aircraft just made a touch-and-go on your runway. How long does the AIM say to wait before you land?
options: No wait is needed in daylight
quiz.why: After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, make sure at least 2 minutes have passed before your takeoff or landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

takeaways: Goal: the slowest, smoothest touchdown, with the wings carrying the weight as long as practical.
Read the surface first: type, slope, NOTAMs, and the corrected landing distance with a margin.
Short-field approach speed, plus half the gust factor, held within 5 knots at the commercial level.
Keep some power on, float 1 to 2 ft up, touch down nose-high on the mains; never chop the throttle.
Nose wheel off, lower it gently, no brakes, and keep moving with power to firm ground.
Tailwind, downhill slope, wake and wind shear all stack up; any doubt, go around early.
cfi_notes: The commercial plus or minus 5 knot window catches pilots who learned to fly the fast side of the private +10/-5. The AFH stabilized-approach list still says +10/-5 [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; train to the ACS number.
The most common error is pulling power to idle in the flare out of normal-landing habit, which drops the airplane in [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Have the student say 'power stays in' on short final.

Most checkrides are flown on pavement, so the examiner will often probe the real-world parts orally: reading the surface, FICON NOTAMs, slope, grass corrections in the POH, and the exit plan to firm ground.
Teach weight transfer as one continuous task of back pressure and power, not a moment. Students who think of it as an event let the nose wheel fall [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Start with low passes in ground effect down a long paved runway to learn the attitude and the small power setting before real touchdowns.

The PHAK still names AC 00-54 (Pilot Wind Shear Guide) as training material [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], but that AC has been cancelled. Teach wind shear from the Aviation Weather Handbook and point out its encounter studies involve large, crew-flown airplanes [[28:267|AWH 22-12]].

PHAK 11-17 gives two different numbers for 10 percent excess landing speed: 'at least 21 percent' and '20 percent' [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. AC 91-79B uses 20 percent as its rule of thumb [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. Either answer shows the idea; don't let students get stuck on it.

Examiners like to ask when a soft-field landing can still become a takeoff: until the weight is on the wheels and the nose wheel is on the surface, field length and obstacles permitting [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
gaps: Airplane-specific numbers (approach speed, flap setting, power setting in the float, grass and wet-grass landing corrections) come from the POH/AFM. The PHAK chart's 20 percent grass note is only a sample [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

S11 asks for elevator 'as recommended by manufacturer' on rollout, and S13 for 'proper position of the flight controls' while taxiing on a soft surface. The sources give the wind control positions [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] and say to keep moving with power, but none gives a back-elevator position for taxiing a nosewheel airplane in mud or snow. Use the POH and CFI technique.
No source here gives landing distance factors for wet grass, mud or snow in small airplanes; PHAK 11-17 says only that soft ground has a significant effect.
No source covers how to physically check a strip (for example a low pass to look at the surface) or how to judge grass height and wetness. That is CFI and local knowledge.
The FAA's wind shear guidance now sits in the Aviation Weather Handbook, whose escape guidance comes from airline studies; there is no small-airplane wind shear recovery procedure in these sources.

activities.title: Name each phase of the soft-field landing
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Round out begins, power stays in
Held 1 to 2 ft up in ground effect
Touchdown on the mains, nose high

activities.title: Longer or shorter landing?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Usually makes the landing roll shorter

items.t: An 8-knot headwind on the sample chart
Mud or snow acting as an obstruction
Crossing the threshold at 80 ft instead of 50 ft

activities.title: Work out the soft-field numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Sample landing chart (Figure 11-32), field at 2,500 ft and 50 F: ground roll 470 ft, total to clear 50 ft 1,135 ft. Dry grass runway: add 20 percent of the total-to-clear figure. What is the grass ground roll?
Same chart at 5,000 ft and 41 F: total to clear a 50 ft obstacle is 1,195 ft. What is the total for a dry grass runway?
Your POH approach speed is 63 KIAS. Wind 200 at 12 gusting 22. What target approach speed do you fly?
items.why: Gust factor = 22 - 12 = 10 knots. Add no more than half: 5 knots. 63 + 5 = 68 KIAS [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Then hold it within 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.D.S7).

items.q: A Cessna 152 chart says to add 10 percent for each 2 knots of tailwind, up to 10 knots. The no-wind landing distance is 1,200 ft and you have a 4-knot tailwind. What distance should you plan?
Landing distance grows about 3.5 percent for each 1,000 ft of altitude. A landing takes 1,000 ft at sea level. About how far will it take at a 4,000 ft field?

activities.title: True or false: power and the float
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Power adds lift without increasing the angle of attack and helps slow the sink rate.
cards.why: True. Power can increase lift without increasing the AOA and slow the descent; propwash gives an instant lift boost [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

cards.s: Ground effect is felt most when the airplane is higher than one wingspan above the ground.
cards.why: False. Ground effect is most realized at heights less than the wingspan [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].

cards.s: At idle, a windmilling propeller can block airflow over the elevator and make the flare hard.
cards.why: True. Low airspeed and a windmilling propeller blocking airflow over the elevator may make it difficult to flare [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

cards.s: If you are slightly high in the landing attitude, lower the nose to get down faster.
cards.why: False. Hold the landing attitude and add enough power to ease the airplane onto the ground [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]. Lowering the nose close to the ground without power can put the nose wheel on first [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

cards.s: Ground effect makes the elevator less effective, so raising the nose takes more effort.
cards.why: True. Ground effect decreases elevator effectiveness and increases the effort needed to raise the nose [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

cards.s: With the wing one-tenth of its span above the ground, induced drag drops by only about 1.4 percent.
cards.why: False. At one-tenth of the span it drops 47.6 percent. The 1.4 percent figure is for a height equal to the full span [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].

activities.title: Put the soft-field landing in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Before the pattern: brief the surface, slope, NOTAMs and corrected landing distance
Downwind: finish the before-landing check before turning base
Final: landing flaps, short-field speed within 5 knots, trimmed, aiming point fixed
Round out and level off 1 to 2 ft up, keeping some power on
Touch down on the mains at the lowest possible speed, nose high
Hold the nose wheel off with back pressure while the wings carry weight
Lower the nose wheel gently and keep rolling with power to firm ground

activities.title: Taxi control positions in the wind
activities.intro: Tap a wind, then the control position the AFH gives for it.

pairs.r: Elevator held full aft to keep the tail down

activities.title: Grass strip, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying N4417K, a four-seat high-wing trainer, with your CFI for commercial checkride practice. You are 10 miles from a non-towered field with a 2,800 ft grass runway, 18/36. Calm-wind runway is 36. The ASOS reports wind 200 at 7.

steps.s: The wind favors runway 18, but your plan and the traffic pattern you briefed were for runway 36. No one else is on the CTAF.
options: Land on 36 as briefed; the wind is light
Self-announce and plan runway 18, into the wind
Land on 36 and add 7 knots to the approach speed
Fly a straight-in to 36 to save time
steps.why: A quartering tailwind adds groundspeed at touchdown, and the first 10 knots add about 21 percent to the landing distance [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. Choose the runway that fits the wind and announce it [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]]. Extra speed only adds float and distance [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

steps.s: Entering downwind for 18, you hear a larger turboprop single announce a touch-and-go on runway 18 just ahead of you.
options: Turn base early to land right behind it
Extend downwind so at least 2 minutes pass after its touch-and-go
Land short of its touchdown point
Continue normally; wake only matters behind jets
steps.why: After a larger aircraft's touch-and-go, vortices can settle along the runway; make sure at least 2 minutes have passed before you land [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. With a light wind they can sit in the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

steps.s: On final at 300 ft AGL you are 9 knots fast and still high.
options: Dive at the aiming point to get down
Go around and set up a new approach
Pull the power to idle and raise the nose
Keep going and burn off the speed in the float
steps.why: Outside 5 knots fails the commercial standard (ACS CA.IV.D.S7), and an approach that becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL calls for an immediate go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Diving toward the aiming point builds a high sink rate [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

steps.s: The second approach is stable. You level off 2 ft up with some power, but the airplane keeps floating and you are now past the first third of the strip.
options: Push the nose down to plant it
steps.why: If you cannot land in the first third of the runway, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. Closing the throttle quickly drops the airplane in [[24:193|AFH 9-22]], and braking can make the nose wheel dig in [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

steps.s: During the go-around you add full power. The airplane is still in ground effect at low speed, and your CFI asks what comes next.
options: Pitch up steeply to climb out of ground effect now
Hold a safe attitude, let speed build, then raise flaps in small steps
Raise all the flaps at once to cut drag
steps.why: Ground effect performance is borrowed; climbing out too soon may leave you unable to climb even at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Once the descent stops, raise the flaps in small increments; raising them all at once can settle the airplane into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

steps.s: Third approach, good touchdown on the mains, nose high. Ahead you see a darker, wet patch, and the wheels start to drag.
options: Lower the nose and brake to stop before the patch
Hold back pressure, add a little power and keep rolling to firm ground
Stop and shut down to avoid getting stuck
Raise the flaps now to put weight on the wheels
steps.why: Hold the nose wheel off with back pressure, stay off the brakes and add power as needed to keep moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Stopping on a soft surface can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], and flap retraction is less important than keeping full control [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a soft-field landing on a turf strip. Compared with a normal landing, what is the major difference in the approach itself?
options: A faster approach to protect against gusts
Some power is carried through the level-off and touchdown
final_quiz.why: The soft-field approach is like the normal approach; the major difference is that a degree of power is used through the level-off and touchdown [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH approach speed is 65 KIAS and the wind is calm. On your commercial checkride, which speed on short final is outside the standard?
final_quiz.why: The commercial standard is plus or minus 5 knots, so 60 to 70 KIAS (ACS CA.IV.D.S7). 72 KIAS is 7 knots fast. On the private checkride (+10/-5) it would have passed (ACS PA.IV.D.S7), and it is inside the wider +10/-5 AFH stabilized-approach criteria [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], which is why the ACS number is the one to train to.

final_quiz.q: No POH speed, VSO 52 knots, wind 270 at 10 gusting 20. What is the highest target approach speed you should plan?
final_quiz.why: 1.3 x 52 = 67.6 knots, plus no more than half the 10-knot gust factor (5 knots) = about 73 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

final_quiz.q: Using the sample chart (Figure 11-32) at 7,500 ft, total to clear a 50 ft obstacle is 1,255 ft and ground roll 520 ft. What is the ground roll on dry grass?
final_quiz.why: Add 20 percent of the total-to-clear figure to the ground roll: 0.20 x 1,255 = 251 ft. 520 + 251 = 771 ft [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]]. 624 ft is the trap of taking 20 percent of the ground roll itself.

final_quiz.q: A landing that takes 1,800 ft on a level runway is planned for a runway with a 1 percent downhill slope. About how far should you expect it to take?
final_quiz.why: A 1 percent downhill slope increases landing distance by about 10 percent (factor 1.1): 1,800 x 1.1 = 1,980 ft [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.7]].

final_quiz.q: You touch down on the mains on a very soft strip, nose high. The nose starts to come down and the airplane is slowing fast. What is the best action?
options: Hold back pressure and add power to keep moving
Let the nose wheel down and brake gently
Close the throttle and stop where you are
Raise the flaps to load the main wheels
final_quiz.why: Keep the nose wheel off with back pressure and use power to control the weight transfer; on a very soft field more power may be needed to keep moving. Brakes can make the nose wheel dig in [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

final_quiz.q: Floating 2 ft over a soft strip, you see a mower start across the far end of the runway. The nose wheel is still off. What can you still do?
options: Nothing; you are committed once you are this low
Apply full power and take off, if field length and obstacles allow
Lower the nose wheel first, then add power
Brake hard and steer around it
final_quiz.why: Before the weight is on the wheels and the nose wheel is on the surface, you can still apply full power and take off, if obstacle clearance and field length permit [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

final_quiz.q: Taxiing a nosewheel airplane off a muddy strip, you want to stop to read the checklist. Why is that a bad idea?
options: The engine will overheat at idle
The flaps must be raised first
Stopping on a soft surface can bog the airplane down, and it takes more power to get moving again
final_quiz.why: Keep continuous motion with enough power, because stopping on mud or snow might bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. More power is needed to start moving than to keep moving [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

final_quiz.q: On final to a grass strip, the runway looks longer and narrower than your usual picture. What does that tell you?
options: Your approach is getting steep, so you are high
Your approach is getting shallow, so you are low
You are on the right glide path
You are drifting off the centerline
final_quiz.why: If the approach steepens, the runway appears longer and narrower; if it gets shallow, the runway looks shorter and wider [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Correct with less power and a lower nose, or more flap [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: You land wing-low in a crosswind in an airplane with nose wheel steering linked to the rudder pedals. What should you do as the nose wheel touches?
options: Add more rudder into the wind
Relax the rudder correction so the airplane does not swerve
final_quiz.why: With linked steering the nose wheel is not lined up with the runway while you hold opposite rudder, so relax that rudder pressure as the nose wheel touches to prevent a swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

final_quiz.q: Arriving at a grass strip, you see a shaft of rain that does not reach the ground and a ring of blowing dust near the runway end. What is the best plan?
options: Land quickly before it reaches the field
Treat it as a likely microburst: hold off or divert, and be ready to go around
Fly the approach 10 knots slow to be ready for a short landing
Land downwind so the gust front pushes you onto the runway
final_quiz.why: Virga at cloud base and a ring of blowing dust are often the only visible microburst clues [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Some microbursts cannot be escaped at low altitude, so be ready for a missed approach at the first indication [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

final_quiz.q: Tower offers you a LAHSO clearance on a short paved runway while you practice soft-field landings. Your computed distance without braking is longer than the ALD. What do you do?
options: Accept, and brake hard if needed
Accept, then reject the landing if it looks tight
Accept, but read back only the runway
final_quiz.why: Accept LAHSO only if you can land and stop within the ALD [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]. The PIC has final authority and is expected to decline if it would compromise safety [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

final_quiz.q: Turning base to final at a grass strip, you overshoot the centerline. Which fix sets up a stall/spin accident?
options: Using inside rudder to skid the airplane around
A coordinated turn with a little more bank, under 30 degrees
final_quiz.why: Stall/spin accidents have happened in the turn to final when pilots tried to rudder the airplane around (skid) to avoid overshooting [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. Never make a skidding turn to correct [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
